title: A routine for a word's meaning
statement: When a reader can decode a word but doesn't know its meaning, teach a routine: mark it, reread its sentence, reread around it, break it into parts.
detail: An IES video on using context, quoted in a reading course's review standard, gives the first steps: mark the unknown word, reread the sentence it is in for clues, and if that doesn't work reread the surrounding sentences (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/teaching-moves/word-solving-for-meaning.md`). The standard adds breaking the word into its parts and, for a child whose home language shares roots, a cognate check, and branches to decoding help only when a diagnostic shows decoding is the barrier. The learner says the meaning in their own words and names the clue that gave it away; the failure the standard names is the instant gloss, which teaches one word and no routine.
against: A curriculum map's note on a grade 3 standard says a child can't use context when the whole domain is unfamiliar, because the surrounding concepts are new too (`downloads/5. Curriculum/Curriculum maps/G3 Standards and Standard components.xlsx`, sheet 'Standard components'), so the routine may fail on a new subject's own terms.

evidence.quote: First is that when we come to that unknown tricky word, we need to mark it in some way. So we can highlight it, we can underline it. Second is we're going to reread the sentence that the unknown word is in and look for clues in that word... If that doesn't work, my third step is I can reread the surrounding sentences.
break the word into morphological parts (prefix/root/suffix)
If diagnostics indicate a decoding barrier, the app may branch to decoding-specific support in a separate support path.
The child must produce a *meaning in their own words* and cite *which clue* gave it away
The failure mode is the **instant gloss**: the tutor supplies the definition and skips transfer, teaching one word and zero routine
